principles:
**Shared requirement, source, and agreement level.** Two principles are in play and they agree at different levels.

*Principle A (F122) — invariants at serialization seams are checked over a described input space, not over hand-picked examples.* Source: py@b08bccfb `tests/core/test_properties.py`, whose module docstring states the rationale in its own words: "Example-based tests check the cases we thought of; these check a *property* of every input Hypothesis can generate, at the two seams where a silent serialization bug would be costly: the domain model's JSON wire form and the config file's persist→reload cycle" (check 10, quoted from the pinned file). Agreement level: **capability** — the template ships generative round-trip testing at its serialization seams, with automatic counterexample minimization and reproducible replay of a discovered failure. The library may vary by ecosystem; the two named seams and the shrink-and-replay behavior are what must agree.

*Principle B (F123) — every command's help text is a reviewed artifact, and an unintended change to it fails the build.* Source: py@b08bccfb `tests/cli/test_help_snapshots.py`, whose F123 evidence line is `assert result.output == snapshot` (check 10, line 36 as the ledger cites) and whose docstring carries the regeneration command `uv run pytest tests/cli/test_help_snapshots.py --snapshot-update` (check 10, line 7). Agreement level: **policy plus one architectural property**. The policy is that help output for every command is compared against a committed reference, drift fails CI, and regeneration is one documented command. The architectural property that must agree is that the reference lives in a **committed file separate from the test source** — py's is `tests/cli/__snapshots__/test_help_snapshots.ambr` (check 10) — because that separation is what makes the change reviewable as a diff in a pull request. Presentation details (file format, macro spelling, review UI) may vary.

**What must vary by ecosystem, and why that is justified rather than drift.** py realizes both principles as pytest plugins injected through fixtures, because pytest's extension model is fixtures and plugins. Rust's `libtest` has no plugin model: a Rust test is a plain function. The same principles are therefore realized as a macro that *is* the test body (`proptest! { … }`) and a macro that *is* the assertion (`insta::assert_snapshot!`). One artifact class is genuinely new on the Rust side: proptest persists a discovered counterexample's seed to a `proptest-regressions/` file next to the test and replays it on later runs, where Hypothesis keeps its example database in an uncommitted `.hypothesis/` cache. Committing that directory strengthens Principle A's replay requirement rather than weakening it — the counterexample travels with the repository instead of living on one developer's machine — and it is the one thing a contributor must be told about. (The persistence mechanism and its `PROPTEST_DISABLE_FAILURE_PERSISTENCE` override are cited from `https://docs.rs/proptest/latest/proptest/test_runner/struct.Config.html` by `raw/opus.md`, retrieved 2026-09-10; this synthesis did not re-fetch that page and did not observe a regressions file being written, because that needs a workspace that does not exist — see `## Engines`.)

**Observable acceptance criteria.** Independent of library choice, the answer is correct only if all of these hold in the built template. Each is a criterion for P03 to prove, not an observation made here.

| # | Criterion |
|---|---|
| 1 | `cargo test`, with no extra flag, feature or environment variable, runs both the property suite and the help snapshots |
| 2 | A deliberately introduced round-trip bug fails the suite with a **minimized** counterexample, not merely the first random input that broke |
| 3 | That failing input is replayable on a later run without a remembered seed |
| 4 | Renaming a CLI flag fails the suite, and the failure output shows a textual diff of old and new help |
| 5 | A newly added subcommand is covered without editing a list of command names |
| 6 | In CI an unreviewed snapshot change **fails** and writes no file into the workspace |
| 7 | Regenerating snapshots after an intentional change is one documented command whose effect is visible in `git diff` |

Criterion 6's mechanism is documented by the maintainer and was verified independently of the raws (check 13): "Insta behaves differently in CI environments. For instance it will not write new snapshot files. This behavior is enabled by the `CI` environment variable. Please ensure that your CI system sets it" (`https://insta.rs/docs/quickstart/`, first retrieved 2026-09-10 and re-fetched by check 13 with identical text on 2026-09-13), and `INSTA_UPDATE`'s default mode `auto` is documented on the same page as "`no` for CI environments or `new` otherwise". GitHub Actions sets `CI=true` on every runner, so this needs no template-side configuration — but that last step is an inference from the runner's documented environment, not something observed in a workflow run here.

**Architectural alternatives compared, before any library was chosen.**

| Alt. | Architecture | Verdict and why |
|---|---|---|
| A1 | No generative testing; table tests over a fixed corpus | Rejected. Cannot satisfy criterion 2 at all. Adopting it would be a deliberate capability drop and would change F122 from "carry the principle" to "declined"; no Rust-specific reason to do so was found |
| A2 | Coverage-guided fuzzing instead (`cargo-fuzz` + `arbitrary`, or `bolero` in fuzz mode) | Rejected on fit. `cargo fuzz` needs nightly and a separate long-lived job; the template is stable-only and criterion 1 requires the default `cargo test` |
| A3 | A strategy-based property runner inside `cargo test` | **Chosen.** The only alternative satisfying criteria 1–3 on stable |
| A4 | `#[test]` plus a hand-written generator loop | Rejected. Re-implements shrinking badly or not at all, in code every template consumer inherits |
| B1 | Spawn the built binary and snapshot its stdout (`insta-cmd`, `trycmd`, `assert_cmd`) | Rejected here, not on quality: it makes the test depend on a build artifact and re-introduces terminal-width and colour sensitivity, and spawning a process per command crosses into R32's built-binary test tier, which this item does not own |
| B2 | Render help in-process from the parsed command definition and snapshot the string | **Chosen**, conditional on R60 — see the paragraph below. Structural analogue of py's `CliRunner().invoke(cli, [*path, "--help"])`: no subprocess, no build artifact |
| B3 | Inline references kept in the test source (`snapbox::str![]`, `expect_test::expect![[…]]`, insta's `@"…"` form) | Rejected *for this principle*. It collapses the reference into the test file, forfeiting the separate-file property Principle B fixes, and the "committed snapshot fixture files" named in this item's value test would cease to exist |
| B4 | External committed snapshot files with a review workflow | **Chosen.** Direct structural analogue of py's `.ambr` file, and insta's default behavior |

**The B2 architecture is conditional on R60, and is stated that way everywhere it appears.** R60 (`cli-parsing-framework`) is open. B2 requires the CLI framework to expose an in-process help renderer and a way to enumerate subcommands. `clap` provides both, and its documentation supplies the determinism pins B2 depends on: `Command::render_long_help` and `Command::get_subcommands` are present in the `Command` method index, and `StyledStr`'s `Display` implementation is documented "Color-unaware printing. Never uses coloring.", with a separate `ansi()` method opting into escape codes (check 9, `https://docs.rs/clap/latest/clap/builder/struct.StyledStr.html` and `.../struct.Command.html`, both HTTP 200, first retrieved 2026-09-10 and re-fetched by check 9 with identical text on 2026-09-13). Colour determinism is therefore a type-level property under clap rather than an environment variable — but only under clap. If R60 selects a framework without an in-process renderer, this item's *architecture* moves to B1 and `insta-cmd` or `trycmd` enters the stack; the principle, the assertion crate, and every gate verdict are unaffected.

**Why the selected design preserves each principle.** For A: `proptest`'s strategies are explicit values rather than a per-type trait, which maps one-to-one onto py's explicit `st.text(st.characters(exclude_categories=("Cs","Cc")), max_size=60)` composition — py deliberately narrows the alphabet so "the property is about *our* round-trip, not the encoder's escaping minutiae" (check 10, quoted from the pinned file), and proptest's regex-backed string strategies express exactly that narrowing. `proptest!` expands to a plain `#[test]` function — both raws state this from the crate's own documentation and neither this synthesis nor either raw compiled it — so the suite is neutral to R32's runner choice as long as that runner still executes `#[test]` functions, which is a conditional on an open item, not a property observed here. For B: `insta::assert_snapshot!` writes its reference to a `.snap` file beside the test, which is the separate-file property, and its CI behavior (criterion 6) needs no wiring. `cargo insta review` supplies criterion 7 with a per-snapshot accept/reject gate; py's `--snapshot-update` accepts everything in the selected scope unconditionally, so this is a place where the Rust port improves on the py baseline while preserving the principle rather than merely matching it.

**Reference implementations, and what each is evidence of.** `rust-lang/cargo` declares `proptest` and uses it for its own dependency-resolver invariants — a rust-lang-org repository choosing this crate for correctness-critical tests, cited by `raw/opus.md` at commit `e7506208ff1b`, retrieved 2026-09-10. `astral-sh/uv` snapshots a CLI whose output contains volatile paths and versions with `insta` and its `filters`/`redactions` features (`Cargo.toml:328` at `a22198b1b536`). `paradigmxyz/reth` declares `insta` and `proptest` in one `[workspace.dependencies]` block (`Cargo.toml:624-626` at `040bef7b319c`), which is the shared-adopter evidence that the two members coexist in one `cargo test` run. `clap-rs/clap` tests its own `--help` output — the most on-point practice evidence in the field — with `snapbox` and inline `str![[…]]` references, which is why `snapbox` is the ranked runner-up and why its loss is argued on the inline-versus-separate-file architecture rather than on quality. All four commit references are carried from `raw/opus.md` and were not re-fetched by this synthesis; the crate-level figures behind the selection *were* re-queried (checks 3–5).

**Fitness gate applicability.** Every gate the prompt lists is answered for every member above; none is silently omitted. Two different kinds of `inapplicable` appear in that table and they must not be read as one.

*Gate 1 is inapplicable by owner ruling, for all three members alike.* On 2026-09-12 the owner ruled (Q4 as superseded by Q7.B) that licence compatibility is not checked for any tool or library this repository uses, depends on, or compiles into its shipped artifact — the repository's licence expression governs its own source and nothing it includes. Gate 1 is therefore not evaluated here for `proptest`, `insta` or `cargo-insta`. The row is kept rather than deleted because `inputs/prompt.md` still lists the gate and its sha256 is cited by the published acceptance record, so the prompt cannot be edited; the prompt's own tier guidance is to state `inapplicable` and the reason rather than drop a gate silently. **Striking the gate leaves nothing about this item unanswered, and the ruling's four carve-outs are each checked against what this decision actually recommends, not waved past.** (1) The repository's own `license = MIT OR Apache-2.0` and any per-file headers are untouched: this decision adds two `[dev-dependencies]` entries and one provisioned binary, and changes no licence text. (2) No third-party file is committed into this repository by this recommendation — every artifact it adds to the tree (`.snap` files under `tests/snapshots/`, `proptest-regressions/*.txt`) is generated by the template's own tests from the template's own code. (3) No member restricts where it may lawfully run, so no functional availability constraint arises. (4) Nothing here is shipped, so no attribution or distribution notice is owed on shipped content: `proptest` and `insta` are `[dev-dependencies]`, which Cargo does not propagate to downstream consumers of the published library, and `cargo-insta` is a separately installed executable that is in no `Cargo.toml`. The crates' declared expressions remain printed in `## Empirical check` as recorded fact, because check 3 and check 7 read them alongside each crate's MSRV, edition and default features; no verdict in this decision rests on them.

*Gates 5 and 6 are inapplicable to one member by that member's form, not by any ruling.* Gate 5's default-features question and gate 6's compile-time question do not apply to `cargo-insta` because it is a provisioned binary, not a linked dependency; the table says so on each row.

**The `filters` feature is recommended conditionally, and its stated premise is unproven.** `raw/opus.md` recommends `insta = { version = "1.48", features = ["filters"] }` so that a crate version appearing in `--help` can be replaced with a stable sentinel, and cites `astral-sh/uv` as a maintained example of that pattern. The premise — that this template's `--help` output will contain the version string — is not established. clap's `Command::help_template` documentation lists `{version}` as a tag a template opts into and describes `help_template` as "overriding the default format", and the fetched page does not quote the default template's text, so what a default `--help` contains is not settled by the evidence gathered here (check 9b). The recommendation therefore is: enable `filters` **only if** the help output P03 actually produces contains a volatile field (a version, a path, an `[env: …]` annotation); otherwise normalize before asserting and keep default features. `json`, `yaml` and `redactions` are not enabled either way; `redactions` would pull `pest` and `pest_derive`, the most expensive option in the feature list, for a plain-text artifact that does not need it.

**The third member, and where the two engines disagreed about it.** `cargo-insta` is adopted for the **local** review workflow, which is uncontested: without it, regeneration falls back to `INSTA_UPDATE=always cargo test`, which reproduces syrupy's blanket-accept weakness — the exact failure Principle B exists to prevent. What is contested is a CI step. `raw/opus.md` recommends `cargo insta test --unreferenced=reject` in the CI test job to fail the build on snapshot files that outlive their tests; `raw/codex.md` says "do not install `cargo-insta` in CI; it is a contributor review tool, while CI's role is to fail on an unreviewed change". This decision takes the narrow position: **the local review tool is recommended; the CI orphan sweep is optional, and P03 decides whether to wire it.** Two reasons. First, criterion 6's unreviewed-change failure needs no tool at all — it is the documented `CI`/`INSTA_UPDATE` behavior (check 13), so the sweep buys only the orphan-file guard, which has no py analogue and is an improvement rather than a carried requirement. Second, `--unreferenced`'s documented default is `ignore` (check 13: "controls what should happen with unreferenced snapshots. The default is `ignore`. Valid values are `ignore`, `warn`, `reject`, `delete` and `auto`"), so the sweep is opt-in by construction and costs nothing to defer. The CI job's shape is owned by R11 and the tool's provisioning by R42; neither is decided here. Revision 2 gave a third reason — that installing an `Apache-2.0` binary into the CI job raised a licence question — and revision 3 withdraws it: the owner's ruling of 2026-09-12 removes licence compatibility from the evaluation of any tool, so that reason no longer exists and the remaining two carry the position on their own.
